newsitem.title: CHINA: China's lacklustre B shares seen rebounding in H2.
newsitem.headline: China's lacklustre B shares seen rebounding in H2.

text.p: Prices of China's B shares have hit bottom after being pushed sharply down by an official crackdown on speculation, and analysts said on Tuesday the hard-currency counters are due for a rebound.

In the past three months, B-share prices had lost nearly 30 percent on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges after hitting year highs in mid-May when Beijing began its crackdown on over-heated stock trading.
"B share prices have hit bottom," one stock analyst with a major Chinese securities house said.
"A rebound is expected in the short term on the back of the low price earnings (P/E) ratios, relaxed governmental control and the improving national economy," she said.
Shanghai's B-share index closed at 71.300 points on Tuesday against a year high of 99.312 points in mid-May and its Shenzhen counterpart ended at 133.25 points against 186.69 before the crackdown.
The foreign-currency counters now had an average P/E ratio of around 15 times with prices of many shares having fallen below the level of their firms' net assets per share.
The rebound could begin in late August or early September, analysts said, when all listed firms are expected to have reported their 1997 interim results. The reporting deadline is August 31.

Analysts polled by Reuters said they thought B shares could regain enough ground to approach the mid-year highs but would lack the momentum to go higher because overall company performances had not improved.

"Investors are waiting until the end of the company interim reporting season before deciding on new strategies," said a B-share trader in Shanghai. "The indices are likely to move in a narrow range before early September, and that is when a new round is expected to begin."
A stock analyst in Shenzhen with J&A Securities said he expected the two B-share indices to gain around 20 to 30 percent in second-half 1997.
Analysts said there were signs the central government was easing its grip on the market after the falls of the past three months, and this would help a rebound.
Beijing's crackdown came after share prices had gained around 50 percent in the first several months of 1997.
The stamp duty on share purchases was raised to 0.5 percent from 0.3 percent, and state banks, state enterprises and listed companies were banned from trading stocks.

China's economy has improved in the past two years with retail price inflation falling to a year-on-year 1.8 percent in the first half of 1997 against 6.1 percent for the whole of 1996 and a post-1949 record of 21 percent in 1994.
China's central bank cut bank interest rates twice, in May and August 1996, and this had helped lift the performance of listed companies, analysts said.

The full impact of the improved economy had yet to be felt on listed firms' results with recent interim reports indicating only slight improvement as a whole and some key firms issuing disappointing results, analysts said.

Shanghai Lujiazui Finance and Trade Zone Development Co Ltd, a key B-share firm in Shanghai, posted net profit of only 179.376 million yuan ($21.6 million) for first-half 1997, compared with 1996's 548.959 million.
"A full recovery of the markets will not occur until March and April next year when the listed firms are expected to post much better results," said a Shanghai-based foreign broker.
